777702.long_answer: Creatine synthesis involves the methylation of guanidinoacetate by the enzyme guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT), a reaction that uses S-adenosylmethionine as the methyl donor. S-adenosylmethionine is produced from the essential amino acid methionine, making methionine critical for creatine synthesis, particularly in the context of GAMT deficiency.

309052.long_answer: The Saguenay–Lac-Saint-Jean region in Quebec, Canada, is notably recognized for a high concentration of rare metabolic disorders due to a founder effect. Among these conditions is 3‐Methylglutaconic aciduria type III, where the increased incidence has been documented and studied within this population.

510628.long_answer: Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) predominantly impairs central vision, leading to difficulties in color discrimination. Patients typically experience red-green dyschromatopsia, a deficit in distinguishing red and green hues, due to the degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and optic nerve fibers that are critical for processing color information.

196118.long_answer: Mutations in the PLCG2 gene, which encodes phospholipase C gamma 2, are linked to PLAID (PLCG2-associated antibody deficiency and immune dysregulation). This condition is characterized by cold-induced urticaria and immunodeficiency, as the mutation affects immune cell signaling and function.

516965.long_answer: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of secondary cold agglutinin disease. This respiratory pathogen induces the production of cold agglutinins—antibodies that can agglutinate red blood cells at cooler temperatures—as part of its immune response.

114060.long_answer: Pick's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder classified under frontotemporal dementia. In this context the question uses a play on words by referencing a famous pin‐up model associated with the American burlesque revival (i.e. Bettie Page) to evoke a similarity with the name “Pick” (as in Friedrich Pick, after whom the disease is named). Thus, the neurodegenerative disease in question is Pick's disease.

287743.long_answer: Surgical resection is the standard treatment for paraganglioma, particularly when the tumor is localized and amenable to complete removal. This approach aims to eliminate the tumor and alleviate any associated symptoms while minimizing the risk of recurrence.

101278.long_answer: Distraction osteogenesis is a surgical method used to gradually lengthen bones. In cases of brachydactyly where shortened phalanges impair function, this procedure involves performing an osteotomy and using a specialized device to slowly stretch the bone, thereby improving hand function.

598908.long_answer: Ischemic stroke is a condition where a lack of blood flow (ischemia) to the brain leads to tissue damage and neurological deficits, typically due to a blockage in the arteries supplying blood to the brain.

102931.long_answer: Chondrosarcoma is a malignant cartilage tumor that can invade surrounding tissues and metastasize to distant sites. It is characterized by its production of cartilage matrix and its potential for local recurrence as well as distant spread, making it distinct from benign cartilage tumors.

246740.long_answer: The FBN1 gene, which encodes the protein fibrillin-1, is located on chromosome 15 (specifically in the 15q21.1 region). Mutations in this gene are responsible for Marfan syndrome, affecting connective tissue structure and function.

497832.long_answer: The FcεRI receptor is a high-affinity receptor on mast cells that specifically binds to the Fc region of IgE antibodies. This binding plays a critical role in the activation of mast cells during allergic responses.

605903.long_answer: Noel Fielding, an English stand-up comedian known for his work on The Mighty Boosh and various stand-up performances, has publicly acknowledged having developmental coordination disorder (often referred to as dyspraxia). This condition affects motor coordination, which Fielding has discussed as part of his personal experience.

573404.long_answer: SETBP1 is the gene in question. Somatic mutations in SETBP1 are associated with atypical chronic myeloid leukemia, while germline mutations in this gene are known to cause Schinzel-Giedion syndrome.

757501.long_answer: Capnography measures end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2), which reflects the effectiveness of chest compressions during CPR by indicating blood flow to the lungs. In patients undergoing CPR—even those experiencing panic attacks—consistent or rising ETCO2 levels imply adequate circulation and better resuscitation efficacy.

801311.long_answer: Dyspnea, or shortness of breath, is a common symptom in both asbestosis and interstitial lung disease. In asbestosis, inhalation of asbestos fibers leads to pulmonary fibrosis, resulting in reduced lung compliance and impaired gas exchange, which manifests as progressive dyspnea. Similarly, interstitial lung diseases cause inflammation and fibrosis of the lung interstitium, leading to the same symptom.

324933.long_answer: Mutations in the AASS gene, which encodes the bifunctional enzyme alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase, disrupt lysine degradation. This disruption leads to hyperlysinemia, a metabolic disorder characterized by the abnormal increase of lysine in the blood.

942306.long_answer: Trisomy 22 is a numerical chromosomal abnormality where there are three copies of chromosome 22 instead of the usual two. This extra copy leads to an autosomal trisomy, as chromosome 22 is one of the autosomes.

552423.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome is primarily caused by mutations in the FGFR2 gene, which resides on chromosome 10. This gene plays a critical role in craniofacial development, and its mutation leads to the abnormal skull and facial bone formation observed in the syndrome.

391648.long_answer: Familial Exudative Vitreoretinopathy is characterized by abnormal retinal vascularization that leads to the leakage of protein-rich fluid. This leakage manifests as a serous exudate in the retina, contributing to exudative detachments.

792409.long_answer: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis, characterized by chronic gingival overgrowth, has been linked to autosomal dominant mutations in the SOS1 gene. This gene encodes a signaling protein that plays a critical role in cell proliferation and growth regulation, making it central to the development of the condition.

297526.long_answer: Tricho–dento–osseous syndrome is caused by mutations in the DLX3 gene, which is located on human chromosome 17. This gene plays a critical role in the development of hair, teeth, and bone.

251353.long_answer: Fasciola jacksoni is a liver fluke that has been documented to infect African elephants. This parasitic trematode locates in the bile ducts or livers of its host, and its occurrence in African elephants is supported by parasitological findings in these animals.

471054.long_answer: Menarche is the term for the first menstrual cycle, marking the onset of puberty in individuals with a typically functioning female reproductive system. In Turner syndrome, due to ovarian dysgenesis and resulting hormonal deficiencies, menarche is often absent, leading to primary amenorrhea.

300982.long_answer: Complete decongestive therapy is a well-established treatment that combines manual lymphatic drainage, compression therapy, specialized exercises, and skin care. This multidisciplinary approach reduces edema and improves lymph flow, which helps to enhance range of motion in patients with lymphedema.

116391.long_answer: Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining is the standard histopathological technique used in muscle biopsies to assess fiber morphology, structure, and the presence of pathological changes in myopathies. Hematoxylin stains nuclei blue while eosin imparts a pink hue to cytoplasmic components, allowing for clear visualization of muscle tissue architecture.

609244.long_answer: Pascual‐Castroviejo syndrome type 1 is also known as COFS syndrome type 1, a severe form of the Cockayne syndrome spectrum. This condition is caused by mutations in the ERCC6 gene (also called CSB), which is located on chromosome 10.

575952.long_answer: Enolase deficiency in several Caucasian families is associated with mutations in the beta-enolase gene (ENO3), which is located on human chromosome 6.

201561.long_answer: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an autoimmune disorder where the immune system mistakenly attacks the peripheral nerves, leading to acute neuromuscular paralysis. It is often triggered by infections or vaccinations and is named after French neurologists Georges Guillain and Jean Alexandre Barre.

908003.long_answer: Mutations in the ACTA1 gene, which encodes skeletal muscle alpha-actin, are associated with severe forms of nemaline myopathy including congenital forms that are incompatible with life. These dominant mutations can disrupt muscle fiber structure and contractility, leading to lethal outcomes in the most severe cases.

547603.long_answer: Thymic carcinoma is an aggressive malignancy, and studies have consistently reported that the 5-year overall survival rate for affected patients falls within the 30–50% range, reflecting the tumor’s aggressive nature and challenges in management.

385015.long_answer: The pancreas is classified as a mixed gland because it has both exocrine functions, producing digestive enzymes secreted via a duct system, and endocrine functions, releasing hormones like insulin and glucagon directly into the bloodstream.

390828.long_answer: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is characterized by two main translocations: PAX3-FOXO1 and PAX7-FOXO1. The PAX3-FOXO1 fusion, resulting from the t(2;13)(q35;q14) chromosomal translocation, is associated with a poorer prognosis compared to the PAX7-FOXO1 fusion.

645310.long_answer: Chronic rhinosinusitis is a condition characterized by long-term inflammation of the sinus and nasal passages. This persistent inflammation can lead to the formation of nasal polyps, which are noncancerous, swollen tissue growths resulting from the ongoing irritation and tissue remodeling in the nasal passages.

308785.long_answer: Multiple lines of clinical evidence for Zeichi-Ceide syndrome point toward an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. In autosomal dominant conditions, only one copy of the mutated gene is needed for an individual to be affected, a mechanism that aligns with the observations seen in families with this syndrome.

100681.long_answer: Fine needle aspiration is a diagnostic procedure where a thin needle is inserted into a breast lump to collect cells for microscopic examination, helping confirm the presence of breast cancer.

304333.long_answer: Hereditary spherocytosis is most commonly associated with defects in spectrin, a key cytoskeletal protein in red blood cells. Spectrin, composed of alpha and beta subunits, contains ATP binding domains that are important for its conformational flexibility and interaction with other membrane and cytoskeletal proteins, contributing to the maintenance of erythrocyte shape and stability.

339050.long_answer: Hereditary hemochromatosis is most commonly associated with the C282Y mutation in the HFE gene. This mutation is responsible for the vast majority of cases and is the primary genetic alteration targeted during diagnostic testing, leading to abnormal iron absorption and accumulation in the body.

732928.long_answer: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are commonly used to alleviate the pain associated with torticollis. They work by reducing inflammation and providing pain relief, making them a first-line treatment option for managing the discomfort and muscle spasms often seen in this condition.

501166.long_answer: Synovial sarcoma is characteristically associated with the chromosomal translocation t(X;18)(p11.2;q11.2), which involves the SS18 gene on chromosome 18 and one of the SSX genes on the X chromosome. This translocation is a key diagnostic marker even when the tumor occurs in atypical locations such as the heart.

440904.long_answer: Fowler's syndrome is a condition seen predominantly in young women, including those with polycystic ovary syndrome. It is characterized by abnormal electromyographic activity of the urethral sphincter, leading to urinary retention.

511744.long_answer: Antiphospholipid syndrome is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the presence of antiphospholipid antibodies, including lupus anticoagulant, which can lead to an acquired resistance to activated protein C. This acquired resistance increases the risk of thrombosis and is a key feature of the syndrome.

695033.long_answer: Pythiosis is an infection caused by the oomycete Pythium insidiosum, which primarily affects skin, vascular, and ocular tissues in both humans and animals.

452476.long_answer: Börjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome is caused by mutations in the PHF6 gene on the X chromosome, and it follows an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance.

795463.long_answer: High-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) is commonly used in infants with bronchopulmonary dysplasia. This mode delivers very small tidal volumes at rapid rates, which helps minimize lung injury by reducing overdistension and cyclic opening and closing of alveoli, a critical consideration in the fragile lungs of these infants.

997135.long_answer: Grover's disease, originally reported by Ralph Wier Grover, is most notably characterized by intense pruritus. This symptom presents as severe itching, often accompanied by small red papules or vesicles, predominantly on the trunk.

986384.long_answer: When Alice in Wonderland syndrome is associated with epilepsy, the treatment involves managing the underlying epileptic activity with antiepileptic drugs. These medications, also known as anticonvulsants, help regulate abnormal electrical activity in the brain, thereby reducing seizure frequency and associated perceptual disturbances.

114901.long_answer: Apert syndrome is primarily caused by a mutation in the FGFR2 gene, which codes for fibroblast growth factor receptor 2. This mutation, typically a missense mutation such as S252W or P253R, leads to abnormal signaling involved in bone development and cranial suture formation, resulting in the clinical features of the syndrome.

503263.long_answer: Hoyeraal–Hreidarsson syndrome is a severe variant of dyskeratosis congenita and is primarily associated with mutations in genes involved in telomere maintenance. The X‐linked form most often features mutations in the DKC1 gene, which encodes the dyskerin protein. In addition, autosomal recessive cases have been linked to mutations in the RTEL1 gene, and mutations in TINF2 have also been reported. These mutations disrupt telomere replication and stability, contributing to the clinical features seen in affected individuals. Genetic testing can identify these mutations to confirm the diagnosis.

597347.long_answer: Cigarette smoking is the most common cause of chronic bronchitis. The chronic exposure to smoke irritants leads to persistent inflammation, mucus overproduction, and structural changes in the airways that characterize the condition.

781212.long_answer: Stanley Greenspan is the child psychiatrist who developed the Floortime approach, a developmental framework used to engage children with conditions such as reactive attachment disorder and autism spectrum disorders through play and interaction.

501777.long_answer: Junctional tachycardia is one of the arrhythmias that can be observed as a sign of digoxin toxicity. Digoxin, a cardiac glycoside, affects the electrophysiological properties of cardiac tissues, particularly enhancing vagal tone and altering conduction through the AV node. In toxic levels, digoxin can induce multiple types of arrhythmias, including premature ventricular contractions, bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, and junctional rhythms (such as junctional tachycardia). While junctional tachycardia may not be the most common presentation, its occurrence is consistent with established medical literature on digitalis toxicity. Therefore, it is considered a sign of digoxin toxicity.

815104.long_answer: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is a hereditary disorder caused by germline mutations in the TP53 gene, a critical tumor suppressor. This mutation results in a significantly increased risk for multiple types of cancer, including sarcomas, breast cancer, brain tumors, and adrenal cortical carcinomas, illustrating the link between inherited genetic defects and cancer predisposition.

926301.long_answer: Xanthelasma are yellowish plaques that form on the eyelids due to the deposition of cholesterol. They are often associated with hyperlipidemia, as elevated levels of lipids in the blood can lead to the formation of these deposits, although they can also occur in individuals with normal lipid levels.

311587.long_answer: At high altitude, reduced oxygen levels activate the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) signaling pathway. This pathway triggers a series of adaptive responses including increased ventilation, elevated erythropoietin production leading to enhanced red blood cell formation, and metabolic adjustments. Together, these mechanisms help maintain oxygen delivery and overall homeostasis under hypoxic conditions.

206204.long_answer: The oculomotor nerve's nuclei are located in the midbrain, specifically at the level of the superior colliculus. Damage or lesions in the midbrain can lead to oculomotor nerve palsy.

179974.long_answer: Multiple familial studies of primary palmar hyperhidrosis, which typically follows an autosomal dominant pattern, have identified a susceptibility locus on chromosome 14. This association supports the notion that genetic factors on chromosome 14 contribute to the aberrant autonomic regulation of sweat glands, which is central to the condition's pathophysiology.

584570.long_answer: Issues with the tympanic membrane can lead to conductive hearing loss, which is a symptom seen in individuals with Marfanoid habitus when middle ear problems occur. Conductive hearing loss results from the disruption of sound transmission due to abnormalities in the tympanic membrane and middle ear structures.

232616.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15. This mutation affects the production of fibrillin-1, leading to abnormalities in connective tissue. The disease commonly impacts the cardiovascular system, potentially resulting in heart palpitations due to aortic dilation and valvular issues.

244992.long_answer: Essential pentosuria is a benign inherited metabolic disorder characterized by the deficiency of L-xylulose reductase, which leads to the accumulation and excretion of L-xylulose in the urine.

491772.long_answer: Hugo Liepmann, a pioneering German neurologist and physiologist, made seminal contributions to the understanding of ideomotor apraxia through his detailed clinical studies and theoretical work. His insights into motor planning and execution mechanisms laid the foundation for our current knowledge of the disorder.

764545.long_answer: British dermatologist Griffiths classified six forms of pityriasis rubra pilaris in the early 1980s. His classification system established distinct clinical subtypes of PRP that have since been used to guide diagnosis and management.

666619.long_answer: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia is linked to mutations in the APOE gene, which is located on human chromosome 19.

856979.long_answer: Babesiosis is caused by Babesia parasites transmitted through tick bites, and its diagnosis and management are within the realm of the Infectious Disease specialty. Infectious Disease specialists have expertise in addressing tick-borne illnesses and utilize appropriate diagnostic tests and treatment regimens for effective patient care.

276083.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome is most often associated with mutations in the FGFR2 gene. A well-documented mutation involves the substitution of the cysteine residue at position 342 (Cys342), which disrupts the receptor's structure and proper disulfide bond formation, leading to abnormal craniofacial development.

873325.long_answer: Osteoporosis pseudoglioma syndrome is characterized by severe osteoporosis and ocular abnormalities, including microphthalmia, and is caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the LRP5 gene. This mutation disrupts Wnt signaling, which is essential for proper bone formation and eye development.

842230.long_answer: Certain cyanobacteria (blue-green algae), notably freshwater species such as Anabaena circinalis, produce saxitoxin. This bacteria synthesizes the potent neurotoxin through its sxt gene cluster, and the toxin is responsible for paralytic shellfish poisoning.

167538.long_answer: Mutations in the NIPBL gene cause Cornelia de Lange syndrome, a condition characterized by growth retardation, microcephaly, limb malformations (often affecting the upper limbs), and distinctive facial features. NIPBL mutations account for the majority of cases of this syndrome and disrupt normal developmental processes.

251155.long_answer: CPVT is a genetic condition in which mutations (commonly in the ryanodine receptor or calsequestrin genes) lead to abnormal calcium handling in cardiac cells. This predisposes individuals to stress- or exercise-induced arrhythmias via an inherent sensitivity to catecholamines. While amphetamines do increase the release of catecholamines and can potentially trigger arrhythmias in susceptible individuals, they are not considered a direct or typical cause of the arrhythmias seen in CPVT. In CPVT, the arrhythmias arise primarily due to the genetic defect and the consequent abnormal response to catecholaminergic stimulation during stress, rather than from amphetamine exposure. Therefore, amphetamines are not routinely involved in the arrhythmias characteristic of CPVT.

497941.long_answer: The most well-established genetic cause of a premature aging syndrome, as seen in conditions like Hutchinson-Gilford Progeria Syndrome, is a mutation in the LMNA gene. This mutation leads to the production of an abnormal form of the lamin A protein (progerin), which destabilizes the nuclear membrane and accelerates aging processes at the cellular level.

557793.long_answer: APOL1 is a gene located on chromosome 22 that has risk variants (notably the G1 and G2 alleles) strongly associated with kidney diseases including hypertensive nephropathy, particularly in individuals of African descent. These kidney diseases can lead to uremic conditions, which are known to cause itching.

378104.long_answer: Mutations in the NLRP3 gene, which encodes the cryopyrin protein, are known to cause a spectrum of autoinflammatory disorders collectively referred to as Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (CAPS). These include familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (FCAS), Muckle-Wells syndrome, and chronic infantile neurologic cutaneous articular (CINCA) syndrome. All of these conditions are characterized by episodic or chronic inflammation, often presenting with periodic fever syndromes among other signs. Thus, the statement that the NLRP3 mutation causes periodic fever syndromes is supported by established biomedical consensus.

583122.long_answer: Interstitial keratitis is an inflammation of the corneal stroma leading to scarring. It is recognized as a late ocular manifestation of congenital syphilis.

144656.long_answer: Pruritus, or itching, is the most commonly reported symptom in mycosis fungoides. This cutaneous T-cell lymphoma typically begins with patches and plaques that cause significant itch, which is a key clinical feature leading to further diagnostic evaluation.

313043.long_answer: Lujan-Fryns syndrome is a rare X‐linked genetic disorder primarily affecting males. It was originally described in a two‐generation Mexican family in which six males were affected, and it is characterized by intellectual disability, a marfanoid habitus, and distinctive facial features.

668267.long_answer: A skin biopsy followed by histopathological examination, often supplemented with immunohistochemical staining, is the gold standard diagnostic method used to differentiate extramammary Paget's disease from conditions like eczema or dermatitis.

320815.long_answer: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune thyroid disease frequently associated with coeliac disease. Both conditions share underlying autoimmune mechanisms, and patients with coeliac disease are at an increased risk of developing this thyroid disorder.

761614.long_answer: The FMR1 gene mutation, characterized by a CGG repeat expansion, is associated with Fragile X syndrome, a condition that often presents with mild intellectual disability along with other physical and behavioral features.

577761.long_answer: Hirschsprung disease is a congenital condition characterized by the absence of enteric ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach’s) and submucosal (Meissner’s) plexuses. This aganglionosis leads to a failure of coordinated intestinal peristalsis, resulting in chronic constipation and colonic dilation.

654735.long_answer: Herpesviruses have an icosahedral capsid with a triangulation number of T=16. This structure is made up of 162 capsomers, with 12 pentons at the vertices and 150 hexons forming the facets, which together encapsulate and protect the viral genome.

113679.long_answer: The RUNX1 gene (formerly known as AML1), which is implicated in acute myeloid leukemia through translocations such as t(8;21), is located on chromosome 21. This chromosomal abnormality is a well-established factor in the development of a specific subtype of AML.

638877.long_answer: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is a widely used brain imaging technique that provides detailed images of brain structures. It is particularly useful for studying structural abnormalities associated with psychiatric conditions such as schizoaffective disorder.

170332.long_answer: Caroline Lavinia Harrison, the wife of President Benjamin Harrison, is the only First Lady known to have died from complications of diphtheria. Her death in 1892 occurred during an era when infectious diseases such as diphtheria were common and vaccination strategies had not yet been developed.

540191.long_answer: Hyperkeratosis is the thickening of the outer layer of the skin due to an increased production of keratin. It can occur as a result of vitamin A deficiency, which disrupts normal keratinization, and as a response to repeated friction or pressure, leading to localized skin thickening.

907738.long_answer: There is no scientific or clinical evidence to support the use of the measles vaccine as part of the treatment for interstitial cystitis. The measles vaccine is developed to provide immunity against measles, a viral infection, and is not indicated for the treatment of inflammatory or chronic bladder conditions like interstitial cystitis. Current treatments for interstitial cystitis involve various approaches like dietary modifications, physical therapy, medications specifically targeting bladder pain and inflammation, and in some cases, more invasive procedures. No established biomedical consensus or clinical trial data supports a therapeutic role for the measles vaccine in managing or treating interstitial cystitis.

142402.long_answer: The gene implicated in pseudoxanthoma elasticum is ABCC6, which is located on chromosome 16. Mutations in this gene cause the mineralization of elastic fibers, a characteristic observed using electron microscopy.

483822.long_answer: Turner syndrome during pregnancy is diagnosed by performing fetal karyotyping. This is typically done using invasive prenatal diagnostic procedures such as chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis, which allow for the analysis of fetal chromosomes to detect the characteristic monosomy X.

135666.long_answer: The hypothalamus is the key brain structure responsible for thermoregulation. In Shapiro syndrome, dysregulation of the hypothalamic control of body temperature is central to the hypothermia observed, despite associations with other brain abnormalities such as corpus callosum agenesis.

131444.long_answer: Follicle-stimulating hormone primarily affects the granulosa cells in ovarian follicles. These cells contain FSH receptors, and insensitivity to FSH directly impacts their proliferation, differentiation, and function in follicular development.

393975.long_answer: Mutations in the FBN1 gene are known to cause acromicric dysplasia, a disorder characterized by short-limb disproportionate short stature. These mutations affect specific domains of the fibrillin-1 protein, leading to the skeletal abnormalities observed in the condition.

437725.long_answer: Uncombable Hair Syndrome Type 2 is caused by mutations in the TGM3 gene, which encodes transglutaminase 3. This gene is located on human chromosome 20, and its dysfunction disrupts proper hair shaft formation, leading to the characteristic uncombable hair phenotype.

861785.long_answer: The SERPINA1 gene, which encodes alpha-1 antitrypsin, is located on chromosome 14, specifically at the 14q32.1 region. Mutations in this gene can lead to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, a disorder affecting the lungs and liver.

913976.long_answer: Polysplenia syndrome is a type of heterotaxy syndrome characterized by multiple small accessory spleens, often associated with dextrocardia and can include biliary atresia. This congenital condition involves abnormal left-right asymmetry during development, leading to malpositioned organs and various cardiac and hepatic anomalies.

765103.long_answer: The disease most directly associated with the dystrophin-associated protein complex is Duchenne muscular dystrophy, which results from a mutation in the DMD gene that encodes the dystrophin protein. The absence or severe deficiency of dystrophin destabilizes the dystrophin-associated protein complex, compromising muscle cell membrane integrity.

546644.long_answer: Vertical transmission ensures that infectious agents are passed directly from parent to offspring, aligning the reproductive interests of both host and microbe. Over time, this intimate association can drive the evolution of a more mutualistic relationship, where the infection evolves reduced virulence or even beneficial traits, thereby transitioning from a pathogenic state to a symbiotic one.

965565.long_answer: BRCA2 is a gene involved in homologous recombination, a key DNA damage repair process. Variants in BRCA2 are well-established to increase the risk of prostate cancer, among other cancers.

385109.long_answer: Injury to the occipital lobe, which houses the primary visual cortex, is known to cause homonymous hemianopia—a condition where there is a loss of vision in the same visual field of both eyes. This specific brain region's impairment disrupts the processing of visual stimuli, leading to the characteristic visual field deficits.

195859.long_answer: Encephalitis lethargica is a neurological disorder first described during the early 20th century. Survivors of the infection often developed post-encephalitic parkinsonism, exhibiting symptoms similar to those of Parkinson’s disease, such as tremor and rigidity. Established research links the viral or immune-mediated impacts of encephalitis lethargica to these lasting neurological impairments.

923039.long_answer: Dental floss is widely recommended for removal of plaque and food particles from between teeth, areas that are hard to reach with a toothbrush. Its use aids in reducing gingival inflammation and can help prevent the progression of periodontal disease by interrupting the buildup of dental plaque.

237212.long_answer: In stomach cancer, lymph nodes are assessed to determine the extent of regional metastasis, which is a critical component of the TNM staging system. The number and location of affected lymph nodes (N stage) provide prognostic information and guide treatment decisions.

156429.long_answer: Trisomy X is characterized by the presence of an extra X chromosome in females, resulting in a total of 47 chromosomes. This karyotype is noted as 47,XXX and is associated with various clinical manifestations, though it is often less severe than other chromosomal aneuploidies.

292237.long_answer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma originates from the epithelial cells lining the pancreatic ducts, which are responsible for secreting an aqueous bicarbonate-rich fluid into the duodenum. This cancer is the most common type of pancreatic cancer and is characterized primarily by its derivation from the ductal cells.

129349.long_answer: Kurt Fearnley was born with spina bifida, a congenital neural tube defect that affects the development of the spinal cord and vertebrae. This condition results in varying degrees of physical disability, which Fearnley has overcome to become a successful Paralympic athlete.

165848.long_answer: Ergocalciferol (vitamin D2) is primarily used for vitamin D supplementation and deficiency correction. There is no well-established evidence or consensus in the biomedical literature indicating that ergocalciferol causes hyperinsulinemia in animals. While vitamin D can influence metabolic functions including insulin secretion and sensitivity, ergocalciferol is not recognized as a direct inducer of hyperinsulinemia. Therefore, the assertion that ergocalciferol causes hyperinsulinemia in animals is not supported by established scientific consensus.

322393.long_answer: The RET proto-oncogene is located on chromosome 10, specifically at the 10q11.2 region. This gene is associated with various thyroid cancers including papillary thyroid cancer and plays a key role in cell signaling pathways.

952812.long_answer: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are commonly used to treat the pain associated with neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome. They help reduce inflammation and alleviate pain, making them a first-line conservative treatment for this condition.

901751.long_answer: Kearns-Sayre syndrome is primarily caused by large-scale deletions in mitochondrial DNA. These deletions disrupt multiple genes necessary for normal mitochondrial function and energy production, leading to the characteristic symptoms of the syndrome.

304785.long_answer: Pediatrics is the medical specialty most likely to treat patients with Down syndrome. Pediatricians oversee the ongoing medical care, developmental assessments, and management of associated health complications common in children with Down syndrome.

999652.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is a genetic disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene, which affects connective tissue. It is associated with a tall, thin body habitus and can lead to skeletal abnormalities, including spinal curvature such as scoliosis.

950110.long_answer: Fetal aortic valvuloplasty is performed during gestation to relieve aortic stenosis, which can lead to hypoplastic left heart syndrome if untreated. By dilating the stenotic aortic valve, the procedure promotes left ventricular growth and function, aiming to mitigate the progression of the disease.

492484.long_answer: Oculodentodigital dysplasia is caused by mutations in the GJA1 gene, which encodes connexin 43. This protein is key for cell communication in various tissues, including those in the eyes, teeth, and fingers. Alterations in its function can contribute to dental anomalies, thereby increasing the risk of dental caries.

242737.long_answer: Gastrocutaneous syndrome, which involves an abnormal connection between the stomach and the skin—often presenting as a congenital anomaly or as a complication of gastrostomy—typically requires surgical correction. Pediatric surgeons specialize in addressing congenital or early-life gastrointestinal defects and are the most likely specialists to treat such cases.

964120.long_answer: Herpes simplex encephalitis is a viral infection that causes inflammation of both the brain tissue and the meninges, particularly affecting the temporal lobes. This damage can lead to the behavioral and cognitive deficits characteristic of Klüver–Bucy syndrome.

447302.long_answer: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) that blocks estrogen receptors. It is used in the treatment of desmoid tumors, as it helps reduce the growth-promoting effects of estrogen on these tumors.

390453.long_answer: Ultrasound imaging is the primary diagnostic modality used to evaluate gallbladder lesions. It can effectively identify masses such as leiomyomas by delineating their size, shape, and echogenic properties, making it the preferred non-invasive approach for initial assessment.

905940.long_answer: The first drug for Gaucher's disease was produced using Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells, which are derived from the Chinese hamster. This mammalian cell line is widely used in biotechnology for the production of recombinant proteins due to its ability to perform post-translational modifications similar to those in humans.

894780.long_answer: The KHK gene, which encodes the enzyme ketohexokinase involved in fructose metabolism, is located on human chromosome 2, not chromosome 5. This enzyme is responsible for phosphorylating fructose in the liver, and its deficiency leads to essential fructosuria, a benign metabolic condition. Therefore, the assertion that chromosome 5 contains the KHK gene is factually incorrect.

683293.long_answer: Primary myelofibrosis causes progressive fibrosis of the bone marrow, leading to extramedullary hematopoiesis. The spleen compensates for the loss of bone marrow function, resulting in significant splenomegaly.

746403.long_answer: Abetalipoproteinemia, also known as Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome, is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the presence of acanthocytes in the blood. It is caused by mutations in the MTTP gene, which encodes the microsomal triglyceride transfer protein necessary for the assembly and secretion of apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins.

687192.long_answer: Pulmonary tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often presents with a set of systemic symptoms including night sweats, fever, weight loss, and a chronic cough. This combination of symptoms, particularly the notable night sweats, is characteristic of tuberculosis rather than typical bacterial pneumonias.

761104.long_answer: BMPR2, which encodes the bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2, is well known for its role in familial pulmonary arterial hypertension and its involvement in bone metabolism through the BMP signaling pathways.

635906.long_answer: Mutations in the OTX2 gene, which plays a key role in early ocular and brain development, are associated with septo‐optic dysplasia and have been found to cause severe bilateral ocular anomalies such as microphthalmia. This established link highlights OTX2's essential function in the development of both the optic structures and the forebrain.

251535.long_answer: Genetic testing for mutations in the ALDOB gene is used to confirm hereditary fructose intolerance. This method accurately identifies the disease-causing mutations and is considered the definitive diagnostic tool for this condition.

329504.long_answer: Double outlet right ventricle with transposition of the great arteries—often described in the context of the Taussig-Bing anomaly—is typically treated with an arterial switch operation. This procedure, frequently combined with closure of the pertinent ventricular septal defect, reestablishes normal anatomical relationships by repositioning the great arteries and coronary arteries to achieve physiological circulation.

704411.long_answer: De Barsy syndrome, an extremely rare autosomal recessive progeroid disorder characterized by cutis laxa, ocular abnormalities, and neurological deficits, has been associated with mutations in the PYCR1 gene. PYCR1 encodes pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase 1, an enzyme involved in proline metabolism, and its mutation is thought to disrupt normal connective tissue development and maintenance, contributing to the syndrome’s clinical features.

631897.long_answer: Inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi) is a well-established inhibitor of extracellular matrix calcification. It prevents the deposition of calcium phosphate crystals by binding to nascent hydroxyapatite, thereby halting the progression of calcification in tissues. In the context of Generalized Arterial Calcification of Infancy, mutations in the ENPP1 gene lead to reduced levels of PPi, contributing to the pathological calcification observed in the disease.

430036.long_answer: Degenerative spondylolisthesis is a condition where one vertebra slips forward over the one below it, potentially compressing nearby nerve roots. This compression can cause radicular pain, and in cases of significant instability or worsening symptoms, spinal fusion surgery may be recommended to stabilize the spine.

340244.long_answer: Congenital sucrase-isomaltase deficiency is a genetic disorder that disrupts the function of brush border disaccharidases, specifically sucrase and isomaltase, leading to an inability to properly digest sucrose and isomaltose. This results in carbohydrate intolerance characterized by gastrointestinal symptoms when sucrose-containing foods are ingested.

657989.long_answer: The disorder known as ichthyosis bullosa of Siemens (or superficial epidermolytic ichthyosis) results from a mutation in the keratin 2e gene located on chromosome 12. It was first described by the German dermatologist Siemens, after whom this condition is eponymously named.

478898.long_answer: A prolactinoma is a type of pituitary adenoma that secretes prolactin. It is a common cause of hyperprolactinemia, which often leads to galactorrhea (abnormal milk production) due to the elevated hormone levels.

422433.long_answer: Benign fasciculation syndrome (BFS) and neuromyotonia are separate neuromuscular conditions. BFS is characterized by benign muscle twitches without significant weakness or abnormal nerve hyperexcitability, while neuromyotonia involves continuous muscle fiber activity due to peripheral nerve hyperexcitability, often with markedly different clinical implications.

918443.long_answer: Short rib–polydactyly syndrome is a congenital skeletal dysplasia characterized by markedly shortened ribs and extra digits. Although management involves a multidisciplinary team (including clinical genetics for diagnosis and counseling, neonatology for supportive care, and sometimes pediatric cardiology or pulmonology due to associated anomalies), the direct treatment and surgical correction of the bony and limb deformities is primarily managed by pediatric orthopedic surgeons.

922563.long_answer: Prednisone is a corticosteroid commonly used to treat Kimura's disease. Its use, especially in prolonged or high doses, may induce a range of side effects including Cushing's syndrome symptoms such as central obesity, moon facies, and hypertension.

332552.long_answer: Clonazepam is a benzodiazepine that enhances GABAergic activity and is commonly used off‐label to manage focal dystonia. Although botulinum toxin injections are the first-line treatment for many focal dystonias, clonazepam is considered in cases where toxin injections are unsuitable or insufficient, helping to reduce the abnormal muscle contractions associated with the condition.

121489.long_answer: Fibrous dysplasia is caused by post-zygotic activating mutations in the GNAS gene, which encodes the stimulatory G protein alpha subunit. These mutations lead to constitutive activation of adenylate cyclase, resulting in abnormal bone development.

597793.long_answer: Agoraphobia is an anxiety disorder characterized by a fear of being in situations where escape may be difficult or help might not be available if panic-like symptoms occur. Chronic benzodiazepine use can lead to a paradoxical increase in anxiety and dependence, and during withdrawal or long-term use, some patients may develop symptoms of agoraphobia.

170655.long_answer: Short-limb skeletal dysplasia with severe combined immunodeficiency, as seen in conditions like cartilage-hair hypoplasia, follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Mutations in the RMRP gene, which are responsible for this disorder, must be inherited from both parents for the phenotype to manifest.

402024.long_answer: Diet can modulate systemic inflammation, which is a key factor in autoimmune conditions like Sjögren's disease. An anti-inflammatory diet—rich in omega-3 fatty acids, antioxidants, and low in saturated fats—may help reduce immune system overactivity and improve symptom severity by lessening inflammatory processes in affected tissues.

132002.long_answer: CYP2U1 is a cytochrome P450 enzyme gene that is involved in fatty acid metabolism and is associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP), specifically SPG56. Mutations in CYP2U1 disrupt normal fatty acid processing, which is thought to contribute to the neurodegenerative features observed in HSP.

228823.long_answer: The BRAF V600E mutation is commonly identified in Erdheim–Chester disease. This mutation leads to a constitutively active BRAF kinase, which in turn activates the MAPK pathway, contributing to the disease's pathogenesis.

731063.long_answer: Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder in which ingestion of gluten leads to damage in the small intestine, causing malabsorption of nutrients such as thiamine. This malabsorption can result in thiamine deficiency, increasing the risk for the development of Wernicke encephalopathy.

442752.long_answer: AMPD1 normally converts AMP to IMP in the purine nucleotide cycle, which is crucial for sustaining ATP regeneration during exercise. In individuals with AMPD1 deficiency, carbohydrate intake boosts glycolytic ATP turnover, leading to rapid AMP accumulation. Without proper deamination, there's insufficient production of downstream metabolites like adenosine, which also helps regulate muscle blood flow. This disruption in energy balance and vasodilation causes a sudden drop in exercise capacity.

443190.long_answer: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis is most commonly linked to mutations in the SOS1 gene. Mutations in this gene affect Ras signaling pathways, leading to abnormal gingival tissue overgrowth.

623138.long_answer: In muscular dystrophies, tissue degeneration primarily results from a genetic defect that leads to the absence or dysfunction of dystrophin, a critical protein that stabilizes muscle cell membranes. Without functional dystrophin, mechanical stress during muscle contraction causes cumulative damage, leading to progressive cell death and replacement by fibrotic and fatty tissue.

741812.long_answer: Liver cirrhosis, a form of chronic liver disease, can lead to hypoalbuminemia which is associated with Muehrcke's lines and is classically linked with Terry's nails. Additionally, advanced cirrhosis may result in hepatopulmonary syndrome, a condition that can manifest with nail clubbing.

206979.long_answer: Coffin–Lowry syndrome is caused by mutations in the RPS6KA3 gene, which encodes the RSK2 protein. This mutation can disrupt normal cardiac function along with other developmental processes, and is associated with the risk of heart failure in affected individuals.

710397.long_answer: Central Hypoventilation Syndrome is colloquially known as 'Ondine's curse,' a name inspired by the play 'Ondine' by Jean Giraudoux. The play draws from the legend of the water nymph Ondine, whose curse causes her lover to lose the ability to breathe automatically, paralleling the loss of autonomic respiratory control seen in the syndrome.

461487.long_answer: The RECQL4 gene, associated with Rothmund–Thomson syndrome, is located on chromosome 8, specifically at band 8q24.3.

630229.long_answer: Waardenburg syndrome is a genetic disorder characterized by congenital sensorineural hearing loss, pigmentary abnormalities of the hair (including poliosis), skin, and eyes, and distinctive facial features due to neural crest cell developmental defects.

680172.long_answer: Rheumatoid nodules are firm, non-tender lumps that are a common extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis. They typically develop in areas exposed to mechanical stress, such as the elbows and other extensor surfaces. Their presence in patients with rheumatoid arthritis is a key clinical finding associated with the disease.

444094.long_answer: Oxytocin is a hormone produced in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary. It plays a key role in maternal bonding, social interactions, and milk production during lactation. Hypothalamic disease can impair its synthesis or release, thereby affecting these functions.

349017.long_answer: Say–Meyer syndrome is a rare congenital disorder that has been reported to follow an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. In this mode, a single copy of the pathogenic variant is sufficient to cause the syndrome, and the clinical presentation may vary among affected individuals.

979645.long_answer: Orthopedic surgery is the medical specialty concerned with conditions of the musculoskeletal system, including the diagnosis and treatment of deformities like familial genu valgum (knock-knees). In cases of familial genu valgum, particularly when the condition has a genetic basis and impacts joint alignment, orthopedic surgeons—especially those specializing in pediatric orthopedics—are typically involved in the evaluation, management, and treatment of the condition.

696655.long_answer: Diagnostic paracentesis is the recommended test for new ascites patients. It involves extracting ascitic fluid for analysis to determine its cause, such as infection (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), malignancy, or cirrhosis-related complications. Key evaluations include cell counts, albumin levels, culture studies, and possibly protein analysis.

325515.long_answer: Based on the established literature regarding syndromes that feature a primary skeletal abnormality, the patella is the bone most consistently reported as affected in conditions sometimes referred to by the eponymous name Hecht Scott syndrome. In this clinical context the patella is described as either hypoplastic or aplastic, which is a key diagnostic feature.

641866.long_answer: Lachiewicz–Sibley syndrome is characterized by congenital abnormalities involving the kidney. It is associated with renal dysplasia and other kidney-specific alterations that affect the structure and function of this organ.

212322.long_answer: Individuals who experience spontaneous episodes of hypothermia and hyperhidrosis are often misdiagnosed with epilepsy because the paroxysmal nature of these autonomic disturbances can mimic seizure activity. In such cases, episodic alterations in temperature regulation and sweating may be erroneously attributed to seizure disorders, leading to a common misdiagnosis of epilepsy.

357449.long_answer: Prenatal diagnosis of cystic hygroma is most commonly performed using ultrasound imaging. This technique is preferred because it is non-invasive, safe for both the mother and fetus, and provides real-time visualization of fetal anatomical structures, which is essential for identifying the characteristic fluid-filled spaces associated with cystic hygroma.

638228.long_answer: Hirschsprung’s disease‐type D brachydactyly syndrome is caused by a contiguous gene deletion – a chromosomal deletion that removes adjacent genes. This deletion affects one or more genes critical for the development of the enteric nervous system (leading to Hirschsprung’s disease) as well as genes involved in digit formation (resulting in brachydactyly type D).

508405.long_answer: The COL1A1 gene, mutations of which lead to osteogenesis imperfecta and can present with features resembling atypical Marfan syndrome, is located on human chromosome 17. Mutations in this gene disrupt the synthesis of type I collagen, which is essential for bone strength and connective tissue integrity.

477384.long_answer: Mutations in the LMNA gene, which encodes for lamin A/C proteins, have been linked to a form of dilated cardiomyopathy characterized by a high incidence of cardiac transplantation and ventricular arrhythmia. These mutations impair the structural integrity of the nucleus, contribute to conduction abnormalities, and increase the risk of sudden cardiac death.

668663.long_answer: Al-Gazali-Donnai-Mueller syndrome results from homozygous mutations in the PUS7 gene, which encodes the pseudouridine synthase 7 enzyme. Because the syndrome is caused by a deficiency in this enzyme’s activity, it is also known as PUS7 deficiency.

585875.long_answer: Phosphoglucomutase 1 (PGM1) converts glucose-1-phosphate to glucose-6-phosphate, a critical step in glycogenolysis. PGM1 deficiency impairs this conversion, affecting both glycogen breakdown and glycosylation, and is recognized as a congenital disorder of glycosylation.

522379.long_answer: Botulinum toxin injections are used to reduce spasticity in hemiparesis patients by blocking the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, leading to muscle relaxation.

540114.long_answer: Nephronophthisis is an autosomal recessive cystic kidney disease and a primary renal ciliopathy. It is notably part of the spectrum of disorders seen in Joubert syndrome and related ciliopathies, where oculomotor apraxia can be one of the neurological manifestations. The involvement of ciliary dysfunction underlies both the renal and ocular motor symptoms observed in these syndromes.

400878.long_answer: Patients with chronic granulomatous disease are particularly susceptible to infections by catalase-positive organisms, with Aspergillus fumigatus being a common fungal pathogen. This fungus takes advantage of the defective respiratory burst in phagocytes, leading to invasive aspergillosis.

892189.long_answer: Feingold syndrome is most commonly caused by mutations in the MYCN gene, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 2 (2p24.1).

160401.long_answer: Leukodystrophy damages white matter in the brain, affecting the neural control of muscles. This often leads to dysphagia, which is difficulty in swallowing, because the coordination and strength of the muscles used in swallowing are compromised.

133020.long_answer: A CBC is commonly performed prior to and during treatment with clozapine, an antipsychotic often used in schizoaffective disorder, because this medication can lead to agranulocytosis—a dangerous drop in white blood cells that increases infection risk.

515055.long_answer: Budesonide is a corticosteroid used to reduce inflammation in lymphocytic colitis. It is also an established treatment for inflammatory bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.

848898.long_answer: In 2012, mutations in the CALR (calreticulin) gene were identified in patients with myeloproliferative neoplasms, including primary myelofibrosis, a disease that commonly causes splenomegaly.

302077.long_answer: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive imaging technique that uses light waves to capture high-resolution cross-sectional images of the retinal layers, making it the standard method for diagnosing macular hypoplasia by assessing the structural integrity of the macula.

574610.long_answer: Current scientific research has not conclusively identified a specific gene mutation associated with Lubani Al Saleh Teebi syndrome. Although the syndrome is recognized as having a likely genetic basis, no definitive mutation has been confirmed in the literature.

631331.long_answer: Antipsychotic drugs, especially the typical (first-generation) antipsychotics, are known to cause dystonia as a side effect. These medications block dopamine D2 receptors, leading to imbalances in the basal ganglia's motor pathways, which can result in the abnormal muscle contractions characteristic of dystonia.

163730.long_answer: Chronic granulomatous disease is characterized by a defect in the NADPH oxidase enzyme complex, which is responsible for generating reactive oxygen species in phagocytes to kill engulfed bacteria. This defect, often due to mutations in the genes encoding components of the enzyme (e.g., gp91phox), leads to impaired microbial clearance and recurrent infections.

393075.long_answer: Combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (CMAMMA) is caused by mutations in the ACSF3 gene. ACSF3 encodes a mitochondrial malonyl‐CoA/methylmalonyl‐CoA synthetase that normally activates the free acids (malonic and methylmalonic acid) by converting them into their CoA esters. In the absence or dysfunction of ACSF3, methylmalonic acid (as well as malonic acid) accumulates, which explains the biochemical profile of CMAMMA.

840102.long_answer: The drug is cyclosporine A, a cyclic peptide used as an immunosuppressant in severe resistant psoriasis. Its established chemical formula is C62H111N11O12, and it works by binding to cyclophilin and inhibiting calcineurin, thereby suppressing T-cell activation.

779438.long_answer: Medication phobia, often referred to as pharmacophobia, is classified as a specific phobia. Specific phobias are a category of anxiety disorders characterized by an irrational and intense fear of a particular object or situation, leading to significant distress and avoidance behaviors.

694094.short_answer: National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
694094.long_answer: The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) is part of the NIH and funds research on brain and nervous system disorders, including studies on encephaloceles. It supports a wide range of research from basic science to clinical studies in this field.

498623.long_answer: Echocardiography, especially transthoracic echocardiography (TTE), is the primary diagnostic tool used to evaluate the structure and function of the pulmonary valve, measure the degree of stenosis, and assess blood flow through Doppler techniques.

378803.long_answer: The GAA gene, which causes Pompe disease by coding for the enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase, is located on chromosome 17, specifically at the 17q25.3 region. This chromosomal location has been consistently reported in scientific literature.

208691.long_answer: Stridor is the high-pitched respiratory sound that occurs due to turbulent airflow through a narrowed airway, typically following laryngospasm. It is commonly observed in conditions such as SBMA (Kennedy's disease), where laryngeal muscle involvement can lead to transient airway obstruction.

545092.long_answer: Neutral lipid storage disease, particularly Chanarin‐Dorfman syndrome, is associated with the accumulation of lipids in various tissues including the thyroid gland. This lipid infiltration can impair thyroid function, leading to reduced hormone production and the development of hypothyroidism, a recognized complication of the disease.

117938.long_answer: Microglia are the primary resident immune cells in the CNS. In the context of HIV infection, these cells become activated and secrete various neurotoxins and proinflammatory cytokines that contribute to neuronal damage and the development of HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders.

406830.long_answer: Moebius syndrome is a congenital condition primarily characterized by facial palsy and abducens nerve involvement leading to ophthalmoparesis, and it is frequently associated with limb anomalies, including arthrogryposis.

787036.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis, an autosomal recessive disorder, is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene. This mutation disrupts chloride ion transport, leading to thick, sticky mucus accumulation in the respiratory system and other organs.

261072.long_answer: Dermatology is the medical specialty that deals with diseases and conditions affecting the skin, including genetic disorders like epidermolysis bullosa simplex. Experts in dermatology are trained to diagnose and manage skin disorders, making them the primary specialists for patients with this condition.

528124.long_answer: In patients with familial hemiplegic migraine, especially those with CACNA1A mutations, even a mild concussion can precipitate a severe neurological complication known as cerebellar edema. This condition involves swelling in the cerebellum, which may lead to significant neurological deficits and is a well-recognized, though rare, complication in this patient population.

132691.long_answer: Multiple system atrophy involves severe autonomic dysfunction that commonly leads to orthostatic hypotension—a sudden drop in blood pressure upon standing. In patients with essential hypertension, the impaired regulatory mechanisms can exacerbate this condition, further compromising cerebral perfusion and increasing the risk of syncope and falls.

380678.long_answer: Prostaglandin E1 is used to maintain a patent ductus arteriosus in infants with interrupted aortic arch. This medication works by relaxing smooth muscle in the arterial wall, allowing blood to bypass the aortic arch obstruction and ensuring adequate systemic blood flow until surgical correction can be performed.

230473.long_answer: Ellis–Van Creveld syndrome is caused by mutations in the EVC and EVC2 genes, which are located on the short arm of chromosome 4 (specifically 4p16).

525709.long_answer: Arrhinia is a congenital condition characterized by the complete absence of the nose, which is classified as a craniofacial malformation. It results from developmental anomalies in the embryologic formation of the facial structures.

998792.long_answer: Madelung's disease, also known as multiple symmetric lipomatosis, is characterized by the abnormal accumulation of adipose tissue generally in the neck and shoulder areas. Treatment primarily involves surgical procedures such as liposuction or excision, which are typically performed by plastic surgeons.

286291.long_answer: Multiple system atrophy (MSA) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive autonomic failure and degeneration of brainstem centers that control automatic breathing. This degeneration can impair respiratory drive, particularly during sleep, leading to central hypoventilation syndrome.

230737.long_answer: Chiari malformation type I involves the downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum. Although often congenital, it can become symptomatic following trauma such as a whiplash injury, leading to neurological symptoms including headaches and neck pain.

928989.long_answer: Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome's most common form is associated with mutations in the CREBBP gene, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 16 (16p13.3).

303981.long_answer: Canine distemper virus often invades the central nervous system, which leads to neurological symptoms such as loss of balance and incoordination in affected dogs.

675571.long_answer: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene, which impairs the peroxisomal beta-oxidation of very long chain fatty acids. Their accumulation disrupts the integrity of myelin, leading to demyelination, particularly in the central nervous system.

362476.long_answer: Beare-Stevenson syndrome, which is characterized by craniosynostosis and cutis gyrata, is caused by a mutation in the FGFR2 gene. This mutation leads to abnormal signaling in fibroblast growth factor pathways, resulting in multiple craniofacial and cutaneous anomalies.

861252.long_answer: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) has been found to be associated with the HLA-B7 serotype. This association supports the role of immune-mediated mechanisms in the disease's pathogenesis.

972207.long_answer: In DSM-IV terminology, mixed receptive‐expressive language disorder is designated with the code 315.39. This diagnosis is used to describe a communication disorder that involves impairments in both language comprehension and language production, and the DSM criteria specifically detail deficits that are not better explained by other neurological, sensory, or cognitive conditions.

970053.long_answer: Tranebjaerg–Svejgaard syndrome is inherited in an X‐linked recessive pattern. This means the gene responsible for the condition is located on the X chromosome, typically causing the syndrome to present predominantly in males, while females often act as asymptomatic carriers.

378925.long_answer: Goiter is the Latin term commonly used to describe a swelling in the neck due to an enlarged thyroid gland. This condition often arises from iodine deficiency, among other causes, and the term has been widely adopted in both medical and scientific literature.

799096.long_answer: Lee Atwater underwent radiation therapy for his astrocytoma, a common treatment modality for malignant brain tumors that uses ionizing radiation to target and kill rapidly dividing cancer cells.

972831.long_answer: Mutations in the CAPN3 gene, which encodes the protease calpain-3, are the most common cause of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD2A) in Euroasia. This mutation affects muscle fiber integrity, leading to the progressive muscle weakness characteristic of the disease.

124948.long_answer: The m.8344A>G mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA^Lys gene (MT-TK) is most commonly associated with MERRF syndrome, leading to impaired mitochondrial protein synthesis and subsequent dysfunction.

899053.long_answer: Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is an aggressive soft tissue tumor most commonly diagnosed in children and adolescents. Its treatment generally involves a multidisciplinary approach, with pediatric oncologists leading management through chemotherapy, surgery, and radiotherapy.

858119.long_answer: ERCC2, also known as XPD, is a subunit of the TFIIH transcription factor complex that plays a critical role in transcription initiation and DNA repair. Mutations in this gene are associated with trichothiodystrophy, thus linking its defective function to the disorder.

870621.long_answer: Allantoin is a key compound produced during the microbial degradation of uric acid in the human gut. It arises from the oxidation of uric acid (often through intermediate steps involving uricase) and is widely recognized in nature as a common building block used in various biosynthetic and metabolic pathways.

819575.long_answer: Basilar invagination is a condition in which the odontoid process of the C2 vertebra migrates upward into the foramen magnum, resulting in the narrowing of the opening. This can compromise vital neural structures and is often associated with craniovertebral junction instability.

833943.long_answer: Madam C.J. Walker was a pioneering African American entrepreneur who developed a range of hair care products designed specifically for African American hair. Her innovations in hair care, including the product known as 'Wonderful Hair Grower', revolutionized the hair care methods and beauty standards within the community.

377888.long_answer: Mutations in the ASS1 gene, which encodes argininosuccinate synthase, cause Citrullinemia Type I—a urea cycle disorder characterized by elevated blood citrulline levels due to impaired ammonia detoxification.

951881.long_answer: Mutations in the ATP1A3 gene are primarily responsible for alternating hemiplegia of childhood and are also associated with dystonia. ATP1A3 encodes a sodium-potassium ATPase critical for neuronal function, and its dysfunction leads to the motor abnormalities observed in these conditions.

446895.long_answer: The Alphavirus genus is the sole remaining genus in the Togaviridae family after the reclassification of Rubella virus into the family Matonaviridae. Alphaviruses are arthropod-borne viruses known to cause diseases such as infectious arthritis, exemplified by chikungunya, and encephalitis in humans.

474702.long_answer: Mutations in the KRT17 gene, which codes for keratin 17, are associated with both Pachyonychia congenita and Steatocystoma multiplex. These mutations disrupt the keratin network, contributing to the clinical manifestations observed in these conditions.

169264.long_answer: Mutations in the MYH3 gene, which encodes the embryonic myosin heavy chain, are linked to distal arthrogryposis syndromes. This genetic alteration disrupts normal muscle development, leading to joint contractures seen in conditions such as Freeman-Sheldon syndrome (a form of distal arthrogryposis).

969880.long_answer: Ectrodactyly with tibia aplasia/hypoplasia, commonly recognized as part of the split-hand/foot malformation with long-bone deficiency spectrum, is strongly associated with genetic alterations affecting chromosome 17, particularly duplications in the 17p13.3 region involving the BHLHA9 gene. This association is well established in the literature as a key genetic mechanism underlying the disorder.

582650.long_answer: Roberts syndrome is a genetic disorder that phenotypically mimics thalidomide embryopathy, displaying limb reduction defects (phocomelia) along with features such as renal dysplasia. The condition is caused by mutations in the ESCO2 gene, which is located on Chromosome 8.

321534.long_answer: Individuals with Stickler syndrome are at a higher risk for eye complications, including retinal detachment, high myopia, and other vitreoretinal abnormalities. Regular examinations by an ophthalmologist are crucial for early detection and management of these conditions to prevent vision loss.

210825.long_answer: Alagille syndrome is predominantly caused by mutations in the JAG1 gene, which is located on chromosome 20p12. This mutation affects the Notch signaling pathway, leading to the multisystem abnormalities characteristic of the disease.

152557.long_answer: A rheumatologist is a specialist in diagnosing and treating inflammatory conditions and autoimmune disorders, including inflammatory myopathies such as perimyositis. These physicians have the expertise required to manage muscle inflammation and related systemic manifestations.

523651.long_answer: Mutations in the PANK2 gene cause pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN), a type of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA). Certain variants, such as those that present with HARP syndrome features, include clinical findings like progressive hair thinning in childhood alongside other neurological and retinal abnormalities.

227339.long_answer: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a type of traumatic brain injury that occurs when the brain is rapidly accelerated or decelerated, such as in a car accident. The shearing forces disrupt the connections between neurons, which can lead to retrograde amnesia—the loss of memories formed before the injury.

283587.long_answer: The ALK gene, located on chromosome 2 (2p23), is associated with anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL). It is frequently involved in chromosomal translocations, notably the NPM1-ALK fusion, which leads to the constitutive activation of ALK's tyrosine kinase activity, playing a key role in oncogenesis.

346532.long_answer: Autosomal dominant GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency, which underlies dopa‐responsive dystonia (Segawa syndrome), is typically treated first with low doses of levodopa. In cases where levodopa therapy is not optimal due to adverse effects or motor fluctuations, dopamine agonists such as the ergot-derived bromocriptine and the non‐ergot pramipexole have been used as second-line treatments. Both agents act directly on dopamine receptors to help alleviate motor symptoms associated with the disorder.

382331.long_answer: The treatment for hypoglycemia in Glycogen Storage Disease type I is uncooked cornstarch due to its slow-release properties that provide a steady glucose supply. One tablespoon of uncooked cornstarch provides approximately 30 calories.

879784.long_answer: Available evidence indicates that children diagnosed with SGFLD syndrome generally experience a favorable clinical course. Although some symptoms may require ongoing supportive management, the syndrome does not typically lead to severe deterioration or reduced life expectancy, and most affected children maintain a stable condition with appropriate care.

619356.long_answer: Oral magnesium supplementation, used to treat hypomagnesemia in patients with Gitelman syndrome, is frequently associated with diarrhea. This side effect is due to magnesium’s osmotic effect in the intestines, which draws water into the bowel and can lead to loose stools.

249522.long_answer: Ethylene oxide is a cyclic ether that is widely used as a sterilizing agent and chemical intermediate. Occupational exposure to ethylene oxide has been classified as carcinogenic (IARC Group 1) and is associated with an increased risk of lung cancer among other cancers.

825150.long_answer: Möbius syndrome is associated with facial paralysis that can lead to malocclusion and other dental issues due to imbalances in muscle function. Orthognathic surgery, which involves repositioning the jaws through maxillary and/or mandibular osteotomies, is indicated to correct these structural misalignments, thereby improving dental function and occlusion.

913596.long_answer: The bleeding disorder assessed by thrombin time is often dysfibrinogenemia, which is linked to mutations in the genes that encode fibrinogen. The fibrinogen gene cluster (FGA, FGB, FGG) is located on human Chromosome 4.

441171.long_answer: GSK3B (glycogen synthase kinase 3 beta) is implicated in bipolar disorder and functions as a key regulator in the Notch signaling pathway. Its modulation by lithium, a primary treatment for bipolar disorder, supports the gene’s relevance in both the disorder and the signaling mechanism.

407006.long_answer: Benign hereditary chorea is most commonly diagnosed through genetic testing that identifies mutations in the NKX2-1 gene. This gene, also known as TITF1, plays a crucial role in the development and function of the brain, thyroid, and lungs, and its mutation is a well-established marker for the condition.

753164.long_answer: Cocaine-induced psychosis is a common mental disorder observed in individuals using cocaine. It is characterized by symptoms such as paranoia, hallucinations, and delusions arising from the drug's impact on dopamine and other neurotransmitter systems.

609049.long_answer: Bone meal, which is processed from animal bones and commonly used as a fertilizer, can be a potential source of prions. If derived from infected animals, it may harbor prions, contributing to the transmission of Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) if introduced into cattle feed or the environment.

928317.long_answer: Lutein is a macular carotenoid with antioxidant properties that has been shown to protect photoreceptor cells from oxidative stress. Its supplementation is thought to help delay the progression of cone dystrophy by filtering harmful blue light and reducing free radical damage in the retina.

188746.long_answer: Grebe dysplasia is an autosomal recessive skeletal disorder caused by mutations in the GDF5 gene. In children of consanguineous parents, the risk of inheriting two copies of the mutated gene is increased, leading to this disorder, which is characterized by severe limb shortening and joint abnormalities.

678211.long_answer: The World Health Organization (WHO) does not classify plasmacytomas as Epstein–Barr virus (EBV)-associated lymphoproliferative diseases. EBV-associated lymphoproliferative disorders typically include a spectrum of conditions, often seen in immunocompromised individuals and primarily affecting B-cell lymphomas that have a known association with EBV infection. Plasmacytomas, on the other hand, are neoplasms of plasma cells and are generally considered a form of plasma cell dyscrasia or multiple myeloma when systemic, rather than being driven by EBV. While EBV infection can occasionally be seen in plasma cell disorders under certain conditions (especially in the context of immunosuppression), it is not a defining factor for the classification of plasmacytomas as EBV-associated lymphoproliferative diseases by the WHO.

241049.long_answer: Cervical spinal stenosis is considered more dangerous because compression in the cervical region affects the spinal cord directly, which can lead to severe neurological deficits including impaired motor function, loss of sensation, and even respiratory complications, unlike lumbar stenosis which primarily compresses nerve roots.

737809.long_answer: Historical accounts of Sakati–Nyhan–Tisdale syndrome indicate that the pediatrics department at the University of Wisconsin–Madison played a central role in its clinical characterization. This department’s involvement provided key clinical insights that helped define the phenotypic spectrum of this rare genetic disorder.

581693.long_answer: Lujan–Fryns syndrome is an X-linked condition, meaning that the gene responsible for the syndrome is located on the X chromosome. This X-linked pattern explains why the syndrome is typically seen in males.

767768.long_answer: Surgical fenestration, including endoscopic or microsurgical approaches, is a potential treatment for symptomatic arachnoid cysts. This procedure involves creating an opening in the cyst wall to allow cerebrospinal fluid to drain, thereby reducing intracranial pressure and alleviating symptoms.

711150.long_answer: Mutations in the GJB2 gene, which encodes the gap‐junction protein Connexin 26, are a well‐established cause of sensorineural hearing loss. In cases of Fryns-Aftimos syndrome, a GJB2 mutation has been identified as leading to deafness, making it the specific gene mutation associated with the auditory phenotype of the syndrome.

559119.long_answer: In Swyer syndrome, individuals have a 46,XY karyotype but nonfunctional gonads, leading to a lack of sex hormones. Estrogen replacement therapy is used to promote the development of female secondary sexual characteristics, such as breast development and uterine growth.

749635.long_answer: Mutations in the ABHD5 gene, also known as CGI-58, cause Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome, a form of neutral lipid storage disease that exhibits Jordans' anomaly, which is characterized by lipid vacuoles in leukocytes.

999115.long_answer: Hereditary hemochromatosis is a genetic disorder causing excessive iron accumulation. The iron overload can trigger oxidative stress and liver damage, thereby increasing the risk of developing porphyria cutanea tarda.

541597.long_answer: CYP21A2 encodes the enzyme 21-hydroxylase, whose deficiency is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Mutations in the CYP21A2 gene, including compound heterozygous forms, disrupt cortisol and aldosterone synthesis, leading to the clinical manifestations of CAH.

579245.long_answer: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene, which encodes a peroxisomal membrane transporter protein essential for the metabolism of very long-chain fatty acids.

716217.long_answer: Dermatitis herpetiformis is a chronic skin condition associated with gluten sensitivity. It is typically diagnosed and treated by dermatologists due to its characteristic skin manifestations and the need for skin biopsies and immunofluorescence studies.

704035.long_answer: Variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease is an invariably fatal neurodegenerative condition. Most patients succumb within 13-14 months after the onset of symptoms due to the progressive and untreatable nature of the prion-induced brain damage.

304715.long_answer: Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, is strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus infection and primarily involves natural killer cells. This lymphoma usually presents in extranodal sites, particularly the nasal region, and is characterized by aggressive clinical behavior.
